subtopic_detail: anticipating a drug level change when a heavy smoker on an antipsychotic metabolised by the same enzyme decides to quit
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a community clinic. A 38-year-old man with treatment resistant schizophrenia has been stable on clozapine for three years with no positive symptoms and is working part time. He smokes thirty cigarettes a day and has decided to stop, motivated by a friend's recent heart attack.

His most recent clozapine level two months ago was in the mid therapeutic range and his white cell count and absolute neutrophil count have been within normal limits at every monitoring visit. He takes no other regular medication, drinks no alcohol and uses no caffeine beyond one coffee daily. He has no constipation and no sedation at present. He tells you he wants to stop abruptly this weekend and asks whether there is anything he should know. His observations and physical examination are within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: No sedation, no sialorrhoea, no abdominal distension, bowels opening daily
data_table.Investigations: Clozapine level in the mid therapeutic range two months ago, white cell count and absolute neutrophil count within normal limits
data_table.Substance use: Thirty cigarettes daily, no alcohol, one coffee daily

lead_in: What is the most important action as he stops smoking?

options.text: Advise him to delay the quit attempt until his mental state has been stable for a further twelve months
options.rationale: He has been stable for three years, and people with severe mental illness die on average two decades early largely from smoking related disease, so deferring a motivated quit attempt is poor care. The near pair is the acutely unwell patient, where timing may reasonably be discussed. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Smoking Cessation in Mental Illness)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Smoking Cessation in Mental Illness

options.text: Monitor the clozapine level closely and reduce the dose as required in the weeks after cessation
options.rationale: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in tobacco smoke induce the cytochrome enzyme that clears clozapine, so stopping removes the induction and levels can rise substantially within one to two weeks, producing sedation, seizures or myocarditis. Level guided dose reduction, often by a quarter to a half over the fortnight after cessation, is what prevents that. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Monitor the clozapine level closely and increase the dose as required in the weeks after cessation
options.rationale: The direction is wrong, because smoking induces rather than inhibits the enzyme, so quitting raises rather than lowers the drug concentration. Dose increases are required when a patient starts or resumes smoking, which is the mirror image of this scenario. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Advise against nicotine replacement therapy because it maintains the enzyme induction he is losing
options.rationale: The induction is caused by combustion products in smoke rather than by nicotine, so replacement therapy does not maintain it and is entirely appropriate. Discouraging it would remove one of the most effective supports for his quit attempt. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Smoking Cessation in Mental Illness)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Smoking Cessation in Mental Illness

options.text: Increase the frequency of white cell and neutrophil monitoring because cessation raises agranulocytosis risk
options.rationale: Haematological monitoring continues on its usual schedule and there is no evidence that quitting smoking affects neutrophil safety. Focusing on the blood count distracts from the pharmacokinetic change that actually matters here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

explanation.summary: Tobacco smoke induces cytochrome P450 1A2 through its polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, and clozapine and olanzapine are both cleared largely by that enzyme. Stopping smoking removes the induction over about one to two weeks, and plasma concentrations can rise by half or more, producing sedation, hypersalivation, seizures and in rare cases myocarditis. The correct response is planned level monitoring with dose reduction, not an argument against quitting and not a dose increase. Nicotine replacement does not maintain the induction because nicotine is not the inducing agent, so it can be used freely, and varenicline is effective and safe in people with stable severe mental illness.
key_points: Tobacco smoke, not nicotine, induces cytochrome P450 1A2
Clozapine and olanzapine levels rise after smoking cessation, often within one to two weeks
Plan level monitoring and dose reduction around a quit date
Restarting or increasing smoking lowers levels and can cause relapse
People with severe mental illness lose roughly two decades of life largely to smoking related disease
explanation.pearls: Check a clozapine level before the quit date and again at one and two weeks afterwards, and reduce the dose pre-emptively by about a quarter when the patient smokes more than twenty cigarettes a day. The same interaction runs in reverse on an inpatient unit: a smoker admitted to a smoke free ward can become toxic within days, and the same patient becomes subtherapeutic again within a week of discharge if they resume.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Smoking Cessation in Mental Illness

subtopic_detail: first line treatment choice for post-traumatic symptoms in a resettled refugee who requires an interpreter and has ongoing visa uncertainty
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a community clinic. A 34-year-old man who arrived in Australia two years ago as a refugee attends with his cousin, who has been translating for him at appointments. He describes nightmares about detention and beatings, waking sweating most nights, and avoiding the news and any uniformed officer.

He startles violently at doors closing, feels constantly on edge, and has stopped attending English classes because crowds frighten him. These symptoms have been present since arrival and have not improved. He has no current suicidal ideation, no psychotic symptoms and no alcohol or other substance use. He sleeps about four hours a night. His visa status is unresolved and he has a hearing in five months. He has no medical comorbidity, takes no medication, and physical examination and observations are within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Anxious, hypervigilant, startles to noise outside the room, no psychomotor retardation, physical examination within normal limits
data_table.Mental state: No current suicidal ideation, no psychotic symptoms, no substance use, sleeping about four hours nightly
data_table.Social: Resettled refugee, unresolved visa status with a hearing in five months, attending with a family member interpreting

options.text: Deferral of all treatment until his visa hearing concludes, with supportive review every month
options.rationale: Ongoing uncertainty maintains symptoms rather than making treatment futile, and there is evidence of benefit from therapy even while immigration matters remain unresolved. Five months of watchful waiting entrenches avoidance and social withdrawal. (Source: Foundation House: Working with Refugee Survivors of Torture and Trauma)
source_refs: Foundation House: Working with Refugee Survivors of Torture and Trauma

options.text: A single session of structured debriefing about the detention experiences followed by watchful waiting
options.rationale: Single session debriefing does not prevent or treat this disorder and may worsen outcomes by provoking distress without the structure to process it. The near pair is trauma focused therapy, which is also exposure based but delivered across multiple sessions with skills training. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian Guidelines for Posttraumatic Mental Health)
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian Guidelines for Posttraumatic Mental Health

options.text: Trauma focused psychological therapy with a professional interpreter engaged for every session
options.rationale: Trauma focused psychological therapy is first line for post-traumatic stress disorder in Australian guidance, including in refugee populations, and outperforms medication as an initial intervention. Using a professional rather than a family interpreter is not a technicality, since a relative both distorts disclosure and is exposed to material that can harm them. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian Guidelines for Posttraumatic Mental Health)
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian Guidelines for Posttraumatic Mental Health

options.text: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor at a standard starting dose with review in four weeks
options.rationale: Medication is an effective second line option and is used when psychological therapy is declined, unavailable or insufficient, but it is not the recommended first step. Starting with a drug also risks framing a response to persecution as a problem located entirely inside the patient. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian Guidelines for Posttraumatic Mental Health)
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian Guidelines for Posttraumatic Mental Health

options.text: A short course of a benzodiazepine at night to restore sleep before any other intervention is started
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are specifically discouraged in this condition because they impair the emotional processing that therapy depends on, worsen outcomes and carry dependence risk. Sleep improves as the disorder is treated rather than the other way round. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian Guidelines for Posttraumatic Mental Health)
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian Guidelines for Posttraumatic Mental Health

explanation.summary: Re-experiencing, avoidance, negative alterations in mood and cognition, and hyperarousal persisting beyond a month after exposure to a traumatic event describe post-traumatic stress disorder. Australian guidance places trauma focused psychological therapy, such as trauma focused cognitive behavioural therapy or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing, ahead of medication as first line treatment. Benzodiazepines are actively discouraged because they interfere with the emotional processing required for recovery. In refugee populations a professional interpreter is essential, because family members both filter disclosure and are themselves harmed by hearing the material, and ongoing visa uncertainty is a reason to treat rather than to wait.
key_points: Trauma focused psychological therapy is first line, ahead of pharmacotherapy
Benzodiazepines worsen outcomes and are not used for this disorder
Use a professional interpreter, not a family member, for trauma disclosure
Unresolved immigration status does not justify deferring treatment
Single session debriefing is ineffective and potentially harmful
explanation.pearls: Ask about head injury and hearing loss in survivors of torture before attributing concentration problems to the psychiatric disorder, since beatings to the head are common and the physical sequelae are routinely missed. When medication is added, sertraline and paroxetine have the strongest evidence base, and prazosin can be considered specifically for nightmares that persist despite therapy.

sources.label: Phoenix Australia: Australian Guidelines for Posttraumatic Mental Health
Foundation House: Working with Refugee Survivors of Torture and Trauma

subtopic_detail: initial response to an adolescent disclosing persistent gender incongruence with coexisting low mood in a general clinic
stem:
You are the registrar in an adolescent mental health clinic. A 15-year-old, assigned female at birth, attends with a parent and tells you that he has identified as male since the age of eleven, uses he and him pronouns with friends and at school, and has asked to be called Jesse for the past three years.

He describes persistent distress about breast development and menstruation, binds his chest daily, and avoids swimming and school changing rooms. He has low mood most days, has stopped playing basketball, and has thoughts that life is not worth living, without plan or intent, and no history of self-harm. He is not using alcohol or other substances and is attending school. His parent says the family is supportive but unsure what to do next and worried about making an irreversible mistake. He is prepubertal in no respect, having completed breast and pubic hair development, and his physical examination and observations are within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Physical examination within normal limits, pubertal development complete
data_table.Mental state: Low mood most days, anhedonia, passive thoughts that life is not worth living without plan or intent, no self-harm history
data_table.Social: Attending school, supportive family, socially transitioned with peers for three years

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Start a gonadotrophin releasing hormone analogue in the clinic today to prevent further distressing development
options.rationale: Puberty suppression is prescribed within a specialist service after multidisciplinary assessment, and it is in any case of limited use once pubertal development is complete. Initiating hormonal treatment in a general clinic bypasses the assessment framework entirely. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital: Australian Standards of Care for Trans and Gender Diverse Children and Adolescents)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital: Australian Standards of Care for Trans and Gender Diverse Children and Adolescents

options.text: Recommend that the family discourage social transition at school until a specialist assessment is completed
options.rationale: Reversing an established social transition is itself an intervention and is associated with worse mental health, and family support is one of the strongest protective factors in this group. He has been living in this role for three years. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Recognising and Addressing the Mental Health Needs of Trans and Gender Diverse People)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Recognising and Addressing the Mental Health Needs of Trans and Gender Diverse People

options.text: Arrange a karyotype and hormonal profile to exclude an underlying disorder of sex development before referral
options.rationale: Endocrine and genetic investigation is indicated when the physical examination or pubertal course is atypical, and his development has been unremarkable. Ordering these tests as a gate before referral introduces delay without changing the pathway. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital: Australian Standards of Care for Trans and Gender Diverse Children and Adolescents)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital: Australian Standards of Care for Trans and Gender Diverse Children and Adolescents

options.text: Assess and treat the depressive symptoms while referring to a specialist gender service for comprehensive assessment
options.rationale: Gender incongruence that has been persistent, consistent and insistent for years with significant distress warrants referral to a specialist multidisciplinary service, which is the Australian pathway for any consideration of medical intervention. Co-occurring depression is assessed and treated in parallel rather than used as a reason to postpone that referral. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital: Australian Standards of Care for Trans and Gender Diverse Children and Adolescents)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital: Australian Standards of Care for Trans and Gender Diverse Children and Adolescents

options.text: Treat the depressive symptoms first and revisit the gender related distress once his mood has fully recovered
options.rationale: Sequencing care this way assumes the gender incongruence is a symptom of the depression, when the distress has been consistent for four years and predates the low mood. Deferring referral prolongs the distress that is contributing to the mood disorder. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital: Australian Standards of Care for Trans and Gender Diverse Children and Adolescents)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital: Australian Standards of Care for Trans and Gender Diverse Children and Adolescents

explanation.summary: Gender dysphoria in adolescence is diagnosed on persistent incongruence between experienced gender and assigned sex causing clinically significant distress, and this young person meets that over four years. Australian standards of care direct referral to a specialist multidisciplinary gender service, where decisions about any medical intervention are made after comprehensive assessment involving the young person and the family. Coexisting mental health problems are common and are assessed and treated concurrently, not used as a precondition for referral or as an explanation that displaces the gender related distress. Family acceptance and the ability to live in the affirmed role are among the strongest protective factors against self-harm in this population.
key_points: Persistent, consistent and insistent incongruence with distress warrants specialist referral
Coexisting depression is treated in parallel, not before referral
Medical interventions are initiated only within a specialist multidisciplinary service
Reversing an established social transition is associated with worse mental health
Endocrine or genetic investigation is reserved for atypical physical findings
explanation.pearls: Ask directly about suicidal ideation and self-harm at every contact, because Australian survey data show that trans and gender diverse adolescents report self-harm and suicide attempts at several times the population rate, and family rejection is the largest modifiable risk factor. Use the young person's stated name and pronouns in the notes and in correspondence, since correspondence that reverts to the birth name is a common reason young people disengage from services entirely.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital: Australian Standards of Care for Trans and Gender Diverse Children and Adolescents
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Recognising and Addressing the Mental Health Needs of Trans and Gender Diverse People

subtopic_detail: weight to give a written advance statement of preferences when a patient is later admitted involuntarily and objects to one medication
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar admitting a 44-year-old woman with schizoaffective disorder who has relapsed after stopping her medication three months ago. She is now under an assessment order after presenting with persecutory delusions and has not slept for four nights.

Eighteen months ago, while well, she completed a written advance statement of preferences with her case manager. It records that if she becomes unwell she does not want olanzapine because of the weight gain she experienced previously, and that she prefers aripiprazole, which she has responded to twice before. She also nominates her sister as the person she wants contacted. She is now refusing all oral medication, saying the staff are poisoning her, and has thrown a chair. Her physical examination and observations are within normal limits, she takes no other medication, and there is no substance use detected on screening.

data_table.Examination: Physical examination within normal limits, no substance detected on urine drug screen
data_table.Mental state: Persecutory delusions about staff, four nights without sleep, agitated and refusing oral medication, threw a chair
data_table.Documentation: Written advance statement of preferences completed eighteen months ago declining olanzapine and preferring aripiprazole, nominating her sister

lead_in: How should the advance statement influence your prescribing?

options.text: Disregard the statement, because compulsory treatment powers override any previously recorded preference
options.rationale: Compulsory treatment authorises treatment without consent but does not extinguish the obligation to consider recorded preferences, and legislation expressly requires reasons when they are departed from. Treating the order as a blanket override is a misreading of the framework. (Source: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act: Advance Statements of Preferences)
source_refs: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act: Advance Statements of Preferences

options.text: Disregard the statement, because it was written more than twelve months ago and is therefore expired
options.rationale: An advance statement of preferences does not lapse after a set interval and remains valid until it is revoked or replaced by the person. Age alone is not a ground for setting it aside. (Source: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act: Advance Statements of Preferences)
source_refs: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act: Advance Statements of Preferences

options.text: Follow the statement only if her nominated support person agrees with the preference it records
options.rationale: The nominated support person is entitled to receive information and to advocate for the patient, but they cannot veto or validate her recorded preferences. The distinguishing relationship is that the statement expresses the patient's own will while the nominated person supports it being heard. (Source: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act: Advance Statements of Preferences)
source_refs: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act: Advance Statements of Preferences

options.text: Follow the statement only if she is currently able to explain and confirm the preference it records
options.rationale: Requiring present capacity defeats the entire purpose of an instrument written in advance precisely for a period when capacity may be impaired. Statements are made while well so they can speak for the person when she cannot. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Supported Decision Making)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Supported Decision Making

options.text: Prescribe her preferred agent unless there is a clinical reason not to, and record the reasoning either way
options.rationale: Australian mental health legislation requires the treating team to make every reasonable effort to give effect to a recorded advance statement of preferences, and to give written reasons when a preference cannot be followed. Aripiprazole has worked for her twice and there is no clinical barrier to using it, so following the statement is both lawful and good practice. (Source: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act: Advance Statements of Preferences)
source_refs: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act: Advance Statements of Preferences

explanation.summary: Advance statements of preferences are a central mechanism of supported decision making in contemporary Australian mental health legislation, and they are written while a person is well so that their wishes carry into periods of compulsory treatment. The treating team must make reasonable efforts to give effect to a recorded preference and must provide written reasons when departing from it. Compulsory status authorises treatment without consent but does not abolish that obligation, and the statement does not expire with time or require the patient's present capacity to be honoured. Here the preferred agent has worked twice before and there is no clinical reason to refuse it, so the statement should be followed.
key_points: An advance statement is made while well and speaks for the person during illness
Reasonable efforts must be made to follow it, with written reasons if departed from
Compulsory treatment status does not override a recorded preference automatically
Statements remain valid until revoked and do not expire with time
A nominated support person advocates for the patient but cannot override the statement
explanation.pearls: Departing from an advance statement is defensible when the preferred treatment is clinically inappropriate or unavailable, but the reason must be documented and given to the patient and their nominated support person, and a vague note that the team preferred another drug will not meet the standard. Honouring preferences where possible is also pragmatic, since patients who see their statements respected are substantially more likely to accept treatment and to engage after discharge.

sources.label: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act: Advance Statements of Preferences
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Supported Decision Making

subtopic_detail: disposition decision for a patient with repeated superficial self-harm presentations who requests admission during a crisis
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar on call to the emergency department at eleven at night. A 26-year-old woman has presented for the fifth time in three months with superficial forearm lacerations after an argument with her partner, sutured by the emergency team an hour ago.

She has a diagnosis of borderline personality disorder made two years ago and attends a weekly dialectical behaviour therapy group, having missed the last two sessions. She describes feeling empty and abandoned, tells you she cut to make the feeling stop, and says she is calmer now that she is here. She denies current intent to end her life and has no plan, and she says she wants to be admitted because she cannot face going home. She has no depressive episode meeting criteria, no psychotic symptoms and no substance use tonight. Her three previous admissions were each followed by an escalation in self-harm on the ward, and her observations and physical examination are within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Superficial forearm lacerations sutured, no other injury, physical examination within normal limits
data_table.Mental state: Distressed and tearful but settling, no current suicidal intent or plan, no psychotic symptoms, no intoxication
data_table.History: Dialectical behaviour therapy weekly with two recent missed sessions, three previous admissions each followed by escalating self-harm on the ward

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Wound care with a structured safety plan and same week return to her usual therapy team
options.rationale: Australian guidance is that admission for this disorder should be brief and reserved for acute risk that cannot be managed otherwise, because longer stays reinforce crisis behaviour and disrupt the therapy that actually reduces self-harm. Collaborative safety planning with rapid re-engagement in the existing programme is the intervention with evidence behind it. (Source: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

options.text: Admission to an acute inpatient unit for a period of containment and observation on the ward
options.rationale: Admission is appropriate for acute suicidal crisis with intent that cannot be managed in the community, and she has neither intent nor plan tonight. Her own history of escalating self-harm during each previous admission is the specific reason to avoid repeating it. (Source: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

options.text: Wound care with a benzodiazepine prescription for crisis use and follow up in the clinic next month
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are discouraged in this disorder because disinhibition increases impulsive self-harm and dependence develops readily. A month long gap also abandons her during the period when re-engagement matters most. (Source: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

options.text: Wound care with initiation of a mood stabiliser to reduce affective instability and review in two weeks
options.rationale: Medication has at best a modest adjunctive role targeting specific comorbid symptoms and no drug is approved for the disorder itself in Australia. Starting one tonight frames the problem as pharmacological and competes with the psychological treatment that works. (Source: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

options.text: Wound care with discharge and advice to present again only if she develops active suicidal intent
options.rationale: Discharging without a plan or follow up leaves her with the same crisis and teaches that presentation must escalate to be taken seriously. The near pair is the structured discharge, which also sends her home but with a written plan and a defined return to care. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Self-harm and Suicidal Behaviour)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Self-harm and Suicidal Behaviour

explanation.summary: Structured psychological therapy is the primary treatment for borderline personality disorder, and dialectical behaviour therapy has the strongest evidence for reducing self-harm. Australian guidance recommends that inpatient admission be brief and reserved for acute suicidal crises that cannot be managed in the community, because longer admissions can reinforce crisis presentations and interrupt the therapy programme. This woman has no current intent or plan, has settled during assessment, and has a documented pattern of escalating self-harm during previous admissions. The intervention with the best evidence tonight is collaborative safety planning followed by rapid return to her existing team, which also treats the missed sessions as the clinical problem they represent.
key_points: Structured psychological therapy, not medication, is the primary treatment
Admission is brief and reserved for acute crisis that cannot be managed otherwise
Prolonged admission can reinforce crisis behaviour and interrupt therapy
Benzodiazepines increase impulsive self-harm through disinhibition
Discharge is structured with a written safety plan and defined follow up, never bare
explanation.pearls: Write the safety plan with the patient rather than for her, naming her own early warning signs, two distress tolerance skills she has already practised, and the specific number to call, because a generic plan handed over at discharge is not used. Treat the missed therapy sessions as the most important clinical finding of the presentation and contact the therapy team directly the next working day, since disengagement typically precedes escalating presentations by several weeks.

sources.label: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Self-harm and Suicidal Behaviour

subtopic_detail: collapse at a dance event with hyperthermia and a low sodium after a recreational stimulant and large volumes of water
stem:
You are the registrar in an emergency department on a Saturday night. An 18-year-old woman is brought in by ambulance from a music festival after collapsing with a seizure lasting ninety seconds. Her friends say she took two tablets sold as ecstasy about four hours ago, danced continuously, and had been drinking a lot of water because she had been told that was the safe thing to do.

She is now drowsy and confused with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 12. Her pulse rate is 136 per minute, blood pressure 106/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air and temperature 40.2 degrees Celsius. Her pupils are 6 mm and reactive and her skin is flushed and sweaty. Sodium is 118 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), creatinine 96 micromol/L (45-90), creatine kinase 3200 units/L (40-200), glucose 6.1 mmol/L, and her venous lactate is 4.4 mmol/L (0.5-2.2). There is no focal neurological deficit and no meningism.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 136 per minute, blood pressure 106/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent room air, temperature 40.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Glasgow Coma Scale 12, pupils 6 mm and reactive, flushed and diaphoretic, no focal deficit, no meningism
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 118 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), creatinine 96 micromol/L (45-90), creatine kinase 3200 units/L (40-200), lactate 4.4 mmol/L (0.5-2.2), glucose 6.1 mmol/L

lead_in: What are the two most urgent interventions?

options.text: Mannitol for the cerebral oedema and a loading dose of phenytoin for seizure prophylaxis
options.rationale: Phenytoin is ineffective for toxic and metabolic seizures, where benzodiazepines are the agent of choice, and mannitol does not address the underlying sodium deficit that is generating the oedema. Neither touches the hyperthermia. (Source: Australasian College for Emergency Medicine: Toxicology Resources)
source_refs: Australasian College for Emergency Medicine: Toxicology Resources

options.text: Hypertonic saline for the sodium and active external cooling for the temperature
options.rationale: Seizure with a sodium of 118 mmol/L is symptomatic hyponatraemia requiring hypertonic saline, and a core temperature above 39 degrees Celsius in this poisoning drives rhabdomyolysis, disseminated coagulopathy and death unless cooled rapidly. These two derangements kill first and both are correctable at the bedside within minutes. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology

options.text: Isotonic saline for the sodium and active external cooling for the temperature
options.rationale: Isotonic fluid is the right choice for the hypovolaemic hyponatraemic patient, but this woman is water loaded rather than depleted and isotonic saline corrects her sodium too slowly after a seizure. Volume loading also risks worsening the cerebral oedema that produced the seizure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology

options.text: Fluid restriction for the sodium and paracetamol for the temperature elevation
options.rationale: Restriction alone is far too slow when a seizure has already occurred, and antipyretics do not work because this hyperthermia is produced by muscle activity and impaired heat dissipation rather than by a raised hypothalamic set point. Both measures treat the numbers without changing the trajectory. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology

options.text: Hypertonic saline for the sodium and dantrolene as the primary measure for the temperature
options.rationale: Dantrolene is reserved for severe hyperthermia that persists despite sedation and aggressive cooling, and relying on it first delays the physical cooling that does most of the work. The distinguishing relationship is that cooling removes heat directly while dantrolene only reduces its production. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology

explanation.summary: This presentation combines two separate life threatening problems produced by the same drug. The stimulant releases antidiuretic hormone and users are often advised to drink freely, so massive free water intake in the presence of impaired excretion produces acute hyponatraemia, cerebral oedema and seizures. Simultaneously, sustained exertion in a hot environment with impaired thermoregulation produces hyperthermia that leads to rhabdomyolysis, coagulopathy and multiorgan failure once the core temperature exceeds about 39 degrees Celsius. Symptomatic hyponatraemia after a seizure requires hypertonic saline, and hyperthermia requires immediate active cooling with benzodiazepines for agitation, with dantrolene held in reserve.
key_points: The drug stimulates antidiuretic hormone release, and advice to drink water compounds it
Seizure with a sodium of 118 mmol/L is symptomatic hyponatraemia requiring hypertonic saline
Hyperthermia here is from muscle activity, so antipyretics do not work
Benzodiazepines are first line for both agitation and toxic seizures
Dantrolene is reserved for hyperthermia refractory to sedation and active cooling
explanation.pearls: Correct the sodium by about 4 to 6 mmol/L acutely to stop the seizure, then respect the usual ceiling of 8 to 10 mmol/L over twenty four hours, since these young patients autocorrect briskly once the drug wears off and the antidiuretic effect ceases. Young women are disproportionately affected by the hyponatraemic presentation, and a normal or near normal sodium at triage does not exclude it because the level continues to fall for hours after the last drink.

sources.label: Australasian College for Emergency Medicine: Toxicology Resources

subtopic_detail: reframing a long history of anxiety and burnout in an adult woman whose difficulties are better explained by lifelong social camouflaging
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in an adult outpatient clinic. A 29-year-old woman has been treated for generalised anxiety disorder and recurrent depression since she was nineteen, with partial response to two different serotonergic antidepressants and a course of cognitive behavioural therapy.

She tells you she has always rehearsed conversations beforehand, copies phrases and mannerisms from colleagues and television characters, and needs two days alone after a work social event before she can function. She has intense and long standing interests in textile history and in timetables, describes seams and fluorescent lighting as physically painful, and has always eaten the same four meals. Her school reports described her as quiet and well behaved with no concerns. She is exhausted after a promotion that requires daily meetings, and she says the anxiety treatment helped her worry less but did not change how draining people are. She has no psychotic symptoms, no substance use and a normal physical examination.

data_table.Mental state: Anxious and exhausted, articulate, reduced spontaneous eye contact, no psychotic symptoms, no current suicidal ideation
data_table.History: Treated for generalised anxiety and recurrent depression since nineteen with partial response to two antidepressants and cognitive behavioural therapy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Add an atypical antipsychotic at low dose for the sensory symptoms and rigid eating pattern
options.rationale: There is no indication for an antipsychotic here, and it would add metabolic risk without addressing sensory processing or routine. Medication in autism targets specific comorbidities rather than the core features. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Reassure her that unremarkable school reports effectively exclude a neurodevelopmental condition in adulthood
options.rationale: Quiet and compliant school behaviour is precisely how autistic girls avoid detection, since the diagnostic threshold historically depended on disruption that they do not produce. Using the absence of childhood concerns to exclude the diagnosis perpetuates the delay. (Source: Autism CRC: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia)
source_refs: Autism CRC: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia

options.text: Refer for a structured developmental history and formal neurodevelopmental assessment by a specialist clinician
options.rationale: Lifelong social effort with rehearsed interaction and imitation, intense circumscribed interests, sensory sensitivity and rigid routines, alongside anxiety that responds only partially to standard treatment, describes autism presenting late in an adult woman. The diagnosis rests on a structured developmental history with collateral rather than on current symptoms alone, so specialist assessment is the correct step. (Source: Autism CRC: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia)
source_refs: Autism CRC: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia

options.text: Switch to a third antidepressant from a different class and review the response in six weeks
options.rationale: A further medication trial addresses the anxiety and depression as though they were the primary problem, when two adequate trials have produced the same partial pattern. It also leaves the exhausting social effort that is driving her presentation entirely unaddressed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Refer for assessment of an emerging personality disorder given her long standing interpersonal difficulties
options.rationale: Personality disorder is a genuine differential and is frequently misapplied to autistic women, but her difficulties are with the mechanics of social processing rather than with unstable relationships, identity or affect regulation. The distinguishing relationship is that camouflaging is an effortful compensation, not an unstable sense of self. (Source: Autism CRC: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia)
source_refs: Autism CRC: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia

explanation.summary: Autistic women are commonly identified late because camouflaging, meaning rehearsed conversation, imitation of others and suppression of self-regulatory behaviour, masks the features that diagnostic criteria were built around. The cost of that effort appears as anxiety, depression and exhaustion, which is why so many women accumulate mood and anxiety diagnoses first and respond only partially to treatment. The clues here are lifelong social effort rather than social fear, intense circumscribed interests, marked sensory sensitivity, rigid routines, and decompensation when social demand rises after a promotion. Diagnosis requires a structured developmental history with collateral information, which is why specialist assessment rather than another medication trial is the right step.
key_points: Camouflaging delays diagnosis in women and is effortful rather than automatic
Anxiety and depression are common consequences and often respond only partially
Quiet compliant school behaviour does not exclude the diagnosis
Sensory sensitivity and rigid routines are core features, not comorbid quirks
Diagnosis requires a structured developmental history, not a cross-sectional interview
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically whether social contact is frightening or merely exhausting, because social anxiety centres on fear of negative evaluation while autistic social fatigue reflects the processing cost of interaction itself, and the two call for different interventions. A late diagnosis remains worthwhile even when no service follows from it, since reframing a decade of perceived personal failure and adjusting workplace and sensory demands often achieves more than the third antidepressant would.

sources.label: Autism CRC: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia

subtopic_detail: explaining a positive bedside inconsistency sign to a patient with sudden leg weakness and normal imaging
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar asked to review a 41-year-old woman on the neurology ward. She developed sudden weakness of the right leg five days ago while carrying shopping, has been unable to weight bear since, and has been admitted for investigation.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and whole spine, nerve conduction studies and inflammatory markers are all within normal limits. On examination there is give-way weakness of right hip flexion, and when you ask her to flex the left hip against resistance you feel firm downward pressure from the right heel. Reflexes are symmetrical and plantar responses are flexor, and sensation is reported as absent below the right groin in a line that stops exactly at the inguinal crease. She is distressed, keen to walk again, and says a doctor told her the scans were normal so there was nothing wrong. She had a right ankle fracture eighteen months ago and has no psychiatric history.

data_table.Examination: Give-way weakness of right hip flexion, involuntary right hip extension on resisted left hip flexion, symmetrical reflexes, flexor plantars, sensory loss ending abruptly at the inguinal crease
data_table.Investigations: Magnetic resonance brain and whole spine within normal limits, nerve conduction studies within normal limits, inflammatory markers within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Document a suspicion of deliberate feigning for secondary gain and arrange covert observation on the ward
options.rationale: Inconsistency signs demonstrate that the movement pathway is intact but not under voluntary control, and they do not distinguish conscious feigning. The distinguishing relationship is that factitious disorder and malingering require evidence of intentional production, which these signs cannot supply. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Functional Neurological Disorder)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Functional Neurological Disorder

options.text: Repeat the spinal imaging with contrast and defer any explanation until the second study has returned
options.rationale: Repeating adequate investigations reinforces the belief that an undiscovered structural lesion explains the symptoms, and each additional negative test makes the eventual explanation harder to accept. The diagnosis rests on positive signs already present rather than on further exclusion. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Functional Neurological Disorder)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Functional Neurological Disorder

options.text: Start an antidepressant for a presumed underlying depressive disorder and review her mood in four weeks
options.rationale: Antidepressants treat comorbid mood and anxiety disorders when they are present, and she has no psychiatric history or current depressive syndrome. Medication is not a treatment for the motor symptom itself. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Explain the positive bedside sign as a rule-in finding and refer for physiotherapy led rehabilitation
options.rationale: Functional neurological disorder is diagnosed on positive signs of internal inconsistency, and involuntary hip extension during resisted contralateral hip flexion is exactly such a sign rather than evidence of feigning. Demonstrating it to the patient as proof that the pathway works, followed by physiotherapy that retrains automatic movement, is the treatment with the best evidence. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Functional Neurological Disorder)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Functional Neurological Disorder

options.text: Explain that the investigations are normal and that no neurological disease has been found, and discharge
options.rationale: A diagnosis of exclusion communicated as an absence leaves the patient with disabling symptoms and no explanation, which is what has already happened and left her distressed. Outcomes depend heavily on how the diagnosis is delivered, and a negative framing predicts poor recovery. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Functional Neurological Disorder)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Functional Neurological Disorder

explanation.summary: Functional neurological disorder is a positive diagnosis resting on demonstrable internal inconsistency, not a label applied when investigations return normal. Hoover's sign, in which hip extension on the weak side returns involuntarily during resisted contralateral hip flexion, shows that the motor pathway is intact while voluntary access to it is not. A sensory level that stops precisely at an anatomical crease and give-way weakness are supporting features. Explaining the diagnosis positively, including demonstrating the sign to the patient, is itself therapeutic, and physiotherapy that retrains automatic rather than deliberate movement is the mainstay of treatment, with psychological therapy added where there are maintaining psychological factors.
key_points: The diagnosis is made on positive signs of inconsistency, not by exclusion alone
Hoover's sign demonstrates an intact pathway with impaired voluntary access
Inconsistency does not indicate feigning and cannot distinguish it
How the diagnosis is explained is a strong predictor of outcome
Physiotherapy retraining automatic movement is the primary treatment
explanation.pearls: Demonstrate the sign with the patient watching and explain it as a problem of the nervous system's software rather than its hardware, since patients who accept the diagnosis at the first explanation have substantially better outcomes than those referred on after months of further testing. Functional and structural disease coexist more often than not, so a previous injury such as her ankle fracture is frequently the physical trigger around which the functional pattern forms, and its presence does not argue against the diagnosis.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Functional Neurological Disorder

subtopic_detail: fever and tachycardia in the third week of an antipsychotic titration where the cardiac and neuroleptic explanations require different immediate actions
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar on an inpatient unit. A 27-year-old man with treatment resistant schizophrenia is on day 18 of a clozapine titration and is now taking 250 mg at night. Over the past two days he has become febrile and lethargic and has vomited twice.

His pulse rate is 126 per minute, blood pressure 102/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 per minute, SpO2 96 per cent on room air and temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius. He has no rigidity, no tremor and no clonus, tone is normal throughout, and he is orientated with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 15. His chest is clear, urinalysis is negative and there is no rash or focal source. White cell count is 13.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0) with an absolute neutrophil count of 8.4 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), eosinophils 0.9 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5), C-reactive protein 68 mg/L (<5), troponin I 640 nanograms/L (<20) and creatine kinase 190 units/L (40-200). The electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia with no ST elevation, and a transthoracic echocardiogram shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 44 per cent with global hypokinesis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 126 per minute, blood pressure 102/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 per minute, SpO2 96 per cent room air, temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Alert with Glasgow Coma Scale 15, normal tone with no rigidity or clonus, chest clear, no rash, no focal infective source
data_table.Investigations: White cells 13.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), neutrophils 8.4 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), eosinophils 0.9 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5), C-reactive protein 68 mg/L (<5), troponin I 640 nanograms/L (<20), creatine kinase 190 units/L (40-200)
data_table.Cardiac: Electrocardiogram sinus tachycardia without ST elevation; echocardiogram left ventricular ejection fraction 44 per cent with global hypokinesis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Cease clozapine, start bromocriptine and dantrolene, and transfer for intensive supportive care
options.rationale: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is the reflex answer to fever on an antipsychotic, but it requires rigidity, altered consciousness and a markedly raised creatine kinase, and his tone is normal with a creatine kinase of 190 units/L. The distinguishing relationship is that one syndrome damages muscle and the other damages myocardium, which is why the troponin and the creatine kinase separate here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Continue clozapine at the current dose, attribute the fever to benign transient pyrexia, and monitor daily
options.rationale: Benign transient fever is genuinely common in the first three weeks and would be a reasonable conclusion with normal cardiac markers, which is what makes this presentation dangerous. A troponin of 640 nanograms/L with new ventricular dysfunction removes that option entirely. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Cease clozapine, start broad spectrum antibiotics for presumed sepsis, and repeat the septic screen in the morning
options.rationale: Culturing and covering for infection is a reasonable parallel action while results are pending, but attributing the picture to sepsis fails to explain the eosinophilia and the new global hypokinesis. Treating this as infection alone delays the cardiac care that determines outcome. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Withhold two doses of clozapine, then resume at a lower dose once the fever has settled, with weekly troponin
options.rationale: A brief interruption followed by reintroduction treats this as a dose related intolerance rather than an immune mediated myocardial injury, and rechallenge after established myocarditis carries a high recurrence rate. Any interruption beyond 48 hours would in any case require full retitration. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Clozapine)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Clozapine

options.text: Cease clozapine permanently, transfer for cardiac monitoring, and involve cardiology in his care
options.rationale: Fever, tachycardia, eosinophilia, a raised C-reactive protein and a markedly raised troponin with new global hypokinesis in the third week of titration is clozapine induced myocarditis, which peaks between days 14 and 21. The drug is stopped permanently because rechallenge carries a high risk of recurrence and death, and cardiac monitoring with specialist input is arranged immediately. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

explanation.summary: Fever during a clozapine titration has three competing explanations that demand different actions, and separating them is the whole task. Benign transient pyrexia is common in the first three weeks and needs only observation, neuroleptic malignant syndrome produces rigidity, autonomic instability, altered consciousness and a markedly raised creatine kinase, and myocarditis produces fever, tachycardia, eosinophilia, a rising C-reactive protein and a raised troponin with new ventricular dysfunction. Here the normal tone and normal creatine kinase exclude the neuroleptic syndrome, while the troponin of 640 nanograms/L with an ejection fraction of 44 per cent and global hypokinesis establishes myocarditis at its characteristic peak between days 14 and 21. The drug is ceased permanently, cardiac monitoring is arranged and cardiology is involved, because rechallenge carries a high risk of recurrent and sometimes fatal myocarditis.
key_points: Clozapine induced myocarditis peaks between days 14 and 21 of titration
Eosinophilia with a rising C-reactive protein and troponin is the characteristic signature
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome requires rigidity and a markedly raised creatine kinase
Benign transient fever is common but never diagnosed in the presence of a raised troponin
Rechallenge after established myocarditis carries a high recurrence risk and is avoided
explanation.pearls: Monitor troponin and C-reactive protein at baseline and weekly for the first four weeks of every clozapine titration, since the diagnosis is made on a rising trend well before the echocardiogram changes, and a troponin above twice the upper reference limit warrants cessation pending assessment. When clozapine must be stopped, plan for cholinergic rebound with agitation, sweating and diarrhoea, and remember that any break of more than 48 hours mandates restarting the titration from a low dose because of the risk of severe hypotension.
